segments.text: I don't know how much Sean has told you.
Not very much.
He was surprised in some cases, but interested in my background.
And said, well, I know somebody who would like to talk to you.
And then you mentioned in your email what your function is, so.
Yeah.
I'm just, I'd like to do background on people I'm interviewing.
So I did a little digging.
And just to see that you worked here in the 90s, is that right?
Did you work here in the 90s?
Is that what the time was?
Yeah, I came in 1985 and retired the first one in 2000.
Then they called me back.
You know, it's like bad cars, they get recalled.
And so I retired again in 2002 and again in 2003.
You can't stay away.
Well, my replacement kept either quitting or not coming.
And at that time, in fact, that's what I came for, is they had the beginning of a separate telecommunication program, separate from electronic, the common base for, I guess,
Yeah, freshman and sophomore, and then they branch out into telecom.
And my role was to develop the telecom part.
Yeah, so when they did call me back, I said, well, I'm retired.
They said, yeah, but you've got juniors that can't graduate because there's nobody offered a course.
Yeah.
Okay, okay.
That's a tricky situation.
It's like they got you there.
They know which button to push.
I wasn't forced to accept.
Right.
So I'm going to be honest.
I know about technology.
I'm not very technologically savvy.
So I was doing a little background research too into your field.
It very quickly turned into another foreign language to me.
But it was so interesting seeing how you were part of the
great technological shift on the university, like you were part of that, you were there, you saw that.
Yeah, well, that period of time, telecom was booming, and the technology was also moving very fast.
But we actually got after the...
second, third year, a separate accreditation for the telecom program, ABET accreditation, so that was good.
Yeah, absolutely.
We were, I think, the second strictly telecom program as opposed to electronic, electricity.
and the first undergraduate to get accredited.
So that was good.
Yeah, absolutely.
Sorry that I'm jumping right into this, but how was that process of getting accredited?
What did that entail?
Oh, that's a very long process.
There's this much paperwork.
They want to know all the description of the program, how many people, students do you have, how many graduates, how many have
are employed, et cetera, et cetera.
But each course, again, a detail, not just a summary.
They want to see everything on the course.
It's a very long preparation process.
And everybody has to do it, but...
Does that go to like, whenever you finish that, does that go to like a national type of?
Yeah, yes.

And so you submit that and so professors of other universities that have a telecom program or something related or are professionally involved in telecom review all of these and then decided, yeah, let's go visit or not.
And so there's a group of three or four people that come and spend two, three days here looking at the labs, looking at the, talking, interviewing the students.
It's a good process, but it takes a lot of time.
Yeah, I can definitely see that.
I would love to get you in touch with this gentleman named Mark Baggett.
He does,
the technological services for the library, but he has access to the supercomputers that we have here.
So I was like, I feel like that's something... Well, that's a different orientation, but...
Can you tell me about where you were born and where you were raised?
I was born in Paris, France, just before World War II in 1937.
We had to, because of the German army invasion of France, we had to move, I think, three or four times during that period to, well, it's...
I was just a kid, I was a little kid, so, but I do remember, suddenly, no, we gotta go, and it was not like next month, it's tomorrow.
Who was in your family at that time?
Well, my kids, I was an only child, but my...
Let's see, yeah, my biological father had to leave because of the war situation and mother was left alone with me.
But later on, I guess, I don't know the details,
My parents divorced, and again, I know he had gone overseas.
And I don't know the details.
Mother didn't want to talk about it.
Right.
But she remarried.
And that, amazingly, that new father of mine, I mean, literally adopted me.
And we went through the war and...
And he took a chance because he was,
I don't remember which level, co-director of a factory.
And of course, Germans took that over and so we left again.
So it was, and all the bombardments and this and that.
Can I ask his name and your mom's name?
I don't know if they want that.
Yeah, I think I'll pass on that.
Sorry.
Well, actually, my biological father, you can have his first name was René.
He was a, he had a, from what I read much later on, he had a PhD in marine biology.
And in fact, went to, that was after the war was over, went to New Caledonia, which is a small island in the Pacific, north of New Zealand, way north, and set up an aquarium there.
He founded the aquarium and became quite famous in his field.
Wow.
It's three, we published three big books.
So, but I actually, no, he left, that was a year and a half, I think.
And I never met him.
Well, that's on the other side of the world, literally.
Right, yeah.
Well, we stayed in touch, writing letters and things.
But your mom, how strong, how strong, wow.
Yeah, she had to, she had to face lots of other problems.
Well, single mother and, you know, the financial input that disappeared, so she had to find a job.
And yeah, and she has her own Ph.D. in sociology.
Wow.
So I had two imposing parents.
Yeah, very educated.
How did you end up...
That was a long circuitous thing.
I studied in France for high school, of course, and then it's like a junior college, but it's specialized.
It was strictly radio and electronics, except for some civics type things.
And then I did my military service in France for three years in their equivalent of the Signal Corps.
So I was radio again.
Since I had done two years of radio school, that made sense for them to put me there.
And after that, I worked at Paris for a year and a half.
And then a friend of mine, who I met in France several times, said, I had mentioned it, he said, you know, you need to come and visit us.
I said, well, yeah, but financial, I think, plus.
He said, well, and then he actually got me a work permit for a year.
So I went there, and the idea was,

well I'll work and I'll save as much money as possible and then I'll play tourist and but the it's not the case anymore but we're talking 1964-65 the telecom technology in the US was easily 10 years ahead of the French one
the telephone network at that time.
You know, there was no internet and digital transmission at that time, but telephone network in France.
It was not a priority, and the telecom was government-owned, like most of Europe.
Yeah, almost, yeah, actually, all of Europe.
The postal service and the telecommunications were government-owned.

And the telephone network, I mean, this is not, it's what, 10 years after the end of World War II, they had a lot of other problems and their decision was, yeah, we have a telephone network, we'll modernize it later, we got to use the money.
for other things, yeah.
So that, I discovered that very quickly, that wow, this is fascinating.
And they, they,
I'm a ham radio operator, so I met some American ham.
I was in New Hampshire for that work.
And one of them, actually, well,
I told him that my work permit was going to expire.
And he said, well, you know, hold on.
He had a small repair and installation shop for mobile radios.
and he was specialized in equipping and maintaining radios for fire departments.
Most of them volunteer fire departments around the south of New Hampshire.
And he said, I had the technician who messed up seriously almost six months ago, and I desperately need somebody.
He said, would you be interested?
Yep.
Well, let's see what I can do.
And so I guess he convinced the immigration folks that I really need somebody and I haven't been able to find a small town in New Hampshire.
And so I got another work permit.
And while I was doing that, I met a young lady who is now my wife, and we've been married for 57 years, I think.
So made the right decision, obviously.
So I worked there, and then same thing, you know, I've got a one-year period.
So I went to immigration in Boston.
and said, is there any way I can renew this?
And I said, no, surely by now we would have been able to find somebody.
And we discussed, and I started the paperwork, and I still remember the lady went to talk to her boss, I guess, and came back and said,
There is one possible.
If you can find a teaching job, you can stay.
We'll give you whatever it's called.
It's not the green card, it's definitely a work permit and also a temporary status, I guess.
But you can't leave New Hampshire.
I said, okay, I can leave.
But that was kind of mid-July.
And I go, ooh, school starts in, what, four weeks?
And that was marvelous.
I was in a little town in Peterborough, New Hampshire, and four different families went all around looking for, you know, do you need me?
And they...
I had essentially given up.
I started making reservations to go back.
And I got one of my friends who was a retired Air Force officer colonel.
called me and said, I got somebody, but you gotta hop.
I said, okay.
Turns out it's a junior college and their math professor, a lady, turned really sick.
And she said,
And I said, well, we need somebody to teach you calculus one and two, right?
Okay, I haven't done that, but I did study that way back.
And so he was the president of the college, not president, director, yeah, must have been president of the college, wrote a letter and said, take that to immigration.
And the same lady said, well, okay, I'm impressed.
So now I had
And that was valid for two years, I think, yeah.
And so, and as I said, I had met my wife there, which, so I had now all kinds of reasons for, it'd be nice.
I asked her, it turned out she's from Germany.
which is interesting.
She's much younger than I am, so we were the start of the year old.
Yeah, when we decided, when we got serious with each other, we went to Europe to meet our respective in-laws.
My mother had lots of friends, a lot of friends.
She was working as a translator for German and English to French.
And I knew several of her friends were Jewish and had serious problems during the war.
And here I come with a German girl.
And I thought, well, wait, she's much younger than I am.
That was not true.
It certainly wasn't her fault, but even, you know, she was born toward, after the war was over.
So I had all kinds of reasons prepared, but I had forgotten how the French, especially the Parisians, think.
And they didn't say, but she's German.
They said, wait, she isn't French.
I wasn't prepared for that.
Yeah, well, I didn't go to the U.S. to specifically look for a French girl.
That was funny.
But we got along with our respective in-laws.
So after the two years in the junior college, I decided to go back to school.
So I got a student visa, University of New Hampshire, electrical engineering, and I got bachelor's and master's from there.
And in the process, somebody said, you know, you're legal with your student status, but you've been here for so long, why don't you try applying for a green card?
And so I did.
And it's when I was a senior at the university, I got a letter saying, okay, we've got the Green Cup, but you've got to register for the draft.
Oh, the middle of the Vietnam War, right?
So I went there, and I still remember the master sergeant who was interviewing me.
He said, yeah, okay, so what's your background, et cetera, et cetera.
He said, you know, I just did three years military.
He looked at me, he said,
Wrong army, buddy.
Yeah.
I admit.
So sign up here.
And then toward the end, because then I had to take a physical and this, and then I came back to him and he said, you forgot to write your birth date.
Yeah, sorry.
I said, wait, you're over 27, so you're right, we need you to register, but unless we declare officially a war, you're too old.
Okay, I guess that's a compliment.
So about, I don't know, several months later, I got the green card, and
Dang, you get to serve in one army and then almost.
Yeah, and I wasn't, I had to think about that.
Do I really want to go to Vietnam and fight over there?
Well, yeah, I think it's worth it.
Besides, my wife had no interest in going back to live in Germany.
So she's staying here.
I think I'm staying here, if possible.
What was, did your wife work?
Yeah, well, when I met her, she was working in a pharmacy, not as a pharmacist, but to help the customers and things.
And then when I decided to go to the university, she, for some reason, followed me.
And she worked in the pharmacy there, but she was working part-time and going to secretary school.
So she was also really busy.
She had a green card already.
She came as, you know what au pair means?
Yeah.
She was a major, I think.
for whom she had babysitted his kids while he was stationed in Germany and done other things.
And so they knew each other very well.
And he said, come on over.
And then she was au pair with him for, I don't know, three years, something like that.
A good amount of time.
Yeah, yeah.
So, university...
Yeah, bachelor's, master's.
And then I worked for what was then General Telephone, which is now Verizon in Massachusetts, just outside of Boston.
I was with them for five years.
and then did something I wanted to do for decades.
I wanted to go overseas and help the people.
I mean, I'm not a doctor, and I'm not, but if they need help with telecom, maybe I can do training and things like that.
And so I had applied to the UN as a specialized agency called the International Telecommunication Union.
And one branch of that is development for less developed countries.
So I applied, I had applied already coming out of the radio school and they said, well, we don't take people at the technician level.
So once I got bachelor's degree, I reapplied and they said, yeah, that's good.
But we prefer, since you're going in those countries, you really need another, I mean, a higher degree.
And it turned out they were absolutely right.
In most of these countries, people will not take...
I don't want to call it orders, but directives from somebody who is not at a higher level than they are.
And they were absolutely right.
So I got my master's and I applied again.

and it's very good we'd like to have you but since you're going to be the specialist over there they call it an expert which is unfortunate because then you go there and well you're expert in everything telecom so no i never worked at those guys they said you were there anyhow so uh you know you you have some experience in the military and some but
again, you need to have a lot of experience, otherwise they're not going to listen to you.
So five years, ooh.
So that's where I went to work for General Telephone.
So after, and while I was there, after the five years, I reapplied.
No, I actually didn't.
I got a letter from the ITU saying we got, we revised your, not revised, we reviewed your application and we noticed you got five years now.
We'd like to have you
there are three possible positions for you.
And one was Equatorial Guinea.
And you know, it's, as the name indicates, they're right on the equator, right in Africa.
And so we think temperature and humidity here is bad, but over there, and they don't have air conditioning.
People were telling me, no, we changed shirts at least twice a day, if not three times.
And I didn't want to go there alone, right?
So by then we had, the twins were born, so no.
Okay, what's the other?
Saudi Arabia with my wife and two daughters?
No, sorry.
Well, we have one in Jamaica.
Ah, that sounds good.
So I took that job.
That was for two years.
They asked me to stay for an extra year.
Then as I was ready to come back to the U.S., my
Boss's boss in Geneva, where the specialized agency is, actually came and said, we started something in Haiti.
We need somebody who speaks French.
Well, I think I qualify with that.
But Haiti, yeah.
He said, hey, how about take your wife and kids and come for, while you help us write the proposal, they can go around.
Well, and that was during Baby Doc, the dictator there.
But Jamaica had its own problem.
The two major political parties, and they were literally fighting each other, and it was, it was, they,
they left foreigners alone, which is good.
But there were a whole region of Kingston, the capital of Jamaica, where, you know, just don't go there.
So we get to Haiti, and it's
I mean, wait, what's going on?
It's so calm here.
Of course, found out later why he'd get out of, you know.
baby dog, full dictatorship, and so you don't mess around.
But I remember walking with him one evening, and we kind of lost our way, and we were in the harbor area, and I thought, oh, that's not a good idea.
And people came to ask us, not for money, or what the heck, are you doing it, but are you lost?
Can we help you?
That's different.
So based on that, many other things.
The job was very interesting.
So after discussion with my wife and then three daughters, we went there for three years, which ended up being six.
So I did a lot of training and organizations.
And then my next post was going to be, still with the UN, it was going to be in Brazil.
And I told him by then, he was my direct boss, now he was in Geneva.
because I was project manager.
And I said, I don't speak Portuguese.
I said, you're going to a research center.
They all speak English.
Good.
But wait a minute.
Can I have some details of, you know, research center?
Yeah, telecom research center.
They're pretty advanced.
They have PhDs.
What do you want me for?
I don't have a PhD.
We've got all kinds of people, researchers.
What we need is something to keep them together, and we need a team leader.
You've been the project manager there for three years.
Okay, if you say so.
So I talked to my wife and the kids.
They said, no.
By that time, the twins were 17.
We are going back to the U.S. You can go where you want.
Okay, get overruled.
So we came back to the U.S.
And well, it's time to look for a job.
And one of our
Specialized Magazine, the IEEE, the Institute of Electronic and Electrical Engineering.
They have many magazines.
And I looked at the job openings, the opening in Texas here, and I said, hmm, for telecoms specifically.
That's unusual.
That sounds good.
So we came and visited.
I got interviewed and I liked it.
So I had to convince all my girls.
And one argument I use is to say, look, this is a nine-month contract, so I've got three months of vacation.
Think of all the time we're going to spend together.
Forty years later, they still remind me.
So when I was spending all this time together...
I say, yeah, it's a nine-month contract, but you do have 12 months of work.
But I mean, I don't regret it at all.
Admittedly, if I had known ahead of time, I probably wouldn't have taken it.
But I'm glad I did.
Yeah, absolutely.
It's, I mean, that...
So, 19 years, 19 and a half years here teaching.
Wow.
We've been everywhere it seems.
The summers were, you know, taken, well, one thing, as I say, telecom, technology was...

increasing and improving very quickly so one part of my summer is to catch up with this because I should teach them and that takes a long time then the books are by definition at least a year behind usually two because it takes a year to write it and then
So I put my own notes based on what I had learned in conferences and in specialized magazines and get copyrights and things like that.
That takes a long time.
And then you have to find a way to get scholarship for these people.
You can't do that during the year because you...
and then also equipment for the lab.
So the summers were pretty busy.
Ellie, my wife, would often say, no, wait a minute, industry, you had at least two weeks guaranteed, right?
Three, but here you can't?
No, I've got to do that.
I figured with all the summer months where I was either not paid at all or half salary,
I essentially worked nine and a half months for free.
Not consecutively, but over the...
Which, again, I don't regret.
When I left, we had three labs, telecom labs.
with equipment, a couple million dollars worth of equipment.
When I came, there was half a lab, and then two courses.
I left, there were nine courses, because each year I would add an additional lab.
That also takes time, by the way.
But I had several offers from industry as I went along,

So, obviously I stayed, and I guess I thoroughly enjoy the relationship with the students, and I felt, you know, former students, some of them still email me, or we meet somewhere, and they're grateful, and we thank you so much.
I thought you hated my test.
I did, but they were very useful.
Yeah.
There's something to be said about that.
I really don't regret it at all.
So that's good.
So the process of, because you said you came and there wasn't like a full program, so you helped build the program.
Yeah, yeah.
That was my role.
That was my, I guess, it was official title in the department.
I don't know if it was true in the college, but I was telecommunication course leader.
because I was developing all those, which is fine.
And I started as an assistant prof, but of course then you got to do a lot of research and publishing.
And I was reminded of that by the...
by the department head, right?
Several of them over the years.
And they said, we love you here, and you're doing a good job, but you've got to do research.
I said, that's not what I came for.
I came for teaching.
Research, I can get a lot better funding in industry.
And they said, yeah, but I can't keep you as assistant prof.
I said, well, any alternative?
And I reminded them, you know, this is an accredited program, right?
And I think I had something to do.
He said, absolutely, but the rule is, which is true.
And he said, well, you can be a lecturer.
I was a lecturer in grad school.
How about senior lecturer?
Let me check.
Then he came back from the dean and said, yeah, okay, you're on.
All right.
But you realize you can never get tenure.
I didn't come for that.
If I'm in the ministry, they can kick me off in two weeks, right?
Here, I've got that list at the end of the semester, so always.
I didn't realize that you would still have to do research.
Oh, yeah.
If you want tenure, there's no research and publishing.
You've got to publish books, or at least articles, and preferably books.
And I had started writing a book on testing telecommunication equipment because, well, I've used those, I've seen those, but...
So the students need it when they get there.
But that takes a lot of time.
And after the second chapter, I had already contacted the editor who was interested.
I said, you know, I know I told you I would do that, but it's either I continue with that at the expense of the students.
You can't do that.
So, that was another reason why it stayed.
Okay, from a perspective,
from a, what's the right word?
Sure, if you have an assistant associate prof, that sounds much better than senior lecturer, but who cares?
This is not what I came here for.
So you really enjoy the teaching aspect of it.
Oh yeah, totally.
Yes, very much so.
And again, you know, I had a close, of course, the telecom...
Typically, I had in each course something like between 20 and 25 students, so you can know them, you can relate both ways.
In fact, I told the seniors the first time, I said, okay, now that you're seniors, you can call me Pierre.
And they loved that.
One of my...
Yeah, I think his title was coordinator.
It's an assistant department head type thing.
who somehow one of the students mentioned that, you know, they call it, and he was a retired Air Force guy, recently retired, and he said, that's not acceptable.
And he told the students, don't ever do that again, because students came and said, oh, yeah.
I said, let me go talk.
And he gave me a hard time.
I said, you're going to lose respect.
The only reason they respect me is if I'm called by my last name, then I, you know.
I said, no, but it's just not done, which is true.
And then the department had overheard the discussion.
He said to him, he said, you're not in
So that continued, and the seniors loved it.
That was their graduation to senior level.
And I, yeah, I,
When I started, I started with, there was an introductory course to telecom for the sophomores, and then a poorly defined telephone request.
network, let's say.
But as I said, that expanded a lot.
I had an industrial advisory board like most programs do, but we were president or equivalent of telephone companies all over Texas and others.
You know, Southwestern Bell, NGT, and...
When I came at first, the first semester, it's a long, I don't know if I'm diverging too much, but these people involved with telephone companies had asked, I guess, the then College of Engineering

I'm trying to remember, well, it won't be an exact thing, but they said, look, we need some telecom people, you know, sure, you're sending us electronic, you know, electrical, electronic people, but then we have to train them for six months, because that's, you don't teach this stuff.
And the then dean of the College of Engineering, this is 1985, right?
Well, no, in fact, it was before I came, so now...
and said, oh, but what you want us to do, that's not university level.
That's a technician program.
No, no, we want engineers, but we want a specialized engineer.
Sorry, we can't do that.
We don't do that here.
And so, I don't remember the details since I wasn't there, I'm just trying to recollect, but somebody in the college said to them, said, wait, why don't you try the engineering technology department?
They are not training people for grad school, they're training people for industry.
So they went, and so in engineering and technology, they said, yeah, well, we can do that.
So they started that one and a half course I'm talking about.
And so when I came, those same people, presidents of different sales companies came, and we had a meeting, and that's,
I introduced myself and said, there are several ways I can orient that.
I did graduate from electronic programs.
Are you interested in them designing circuits or are you interested in them applying the existing equipment in the best possible?
I said, circuits we have from electrical engineers.
We got plenty of those.
That's not what we want.
We don't want to have spent six months training everybody.
Oh, good, that's where I came from, system side.
And they were, so that I developed the different courses based on my experience, but also saying, okay, but what do you people want more specifically?
What kind of technology are you using?
And so we started things to respond to that.
Because they were pleased with the department and with the graduates, they started offering some equipment.
And I remember that was after several years.
But I kept a relationship with those guys, and we were fairly close.
And I asked one of them, I said, I won't mention the company, but I said, you know, I'm impressed by the amount of equipment you're giving us and the scholarships.
He said, well, there's something special about your program.
We noticed your equipment within a semester or so has been set up and is working.
We know you're doing something with it.
There are other places where that thing just sits there for whatever reason, for years.
I said, well, I can keep doing that.
Keep doing that.
So, and yeah, I mean, and the scholarships, too.
That was...
And because, well, okay, I get some credit there, because the program was good and correctly oriented.
And because telecom was booming at that time, all my students, if they had C or better, had a job before they graduated.
Some of them went on the internship, but even besides that, they came here and they would tell, which didn't please the recruiting folks over there.
They said, no, no, no, we want to talk to the engineering technology telecom group.
But we have many.
Yes, we know.
Everybody got a job.
You had to have a seat.
That's fair enough, right?
That's impressive.
One of the petroleum company, they had their own, like all of a large corporation, they have their own telecom network, privately owned.
So they have a telecom group that takes care of that.
And their director of that group...
Now you ask them, I would go and visit them, that particular thing was in Chicago.
And I asked him over dinner, he said, you know, I'm really grateful that you are hiring my C students.
And they said, well, but I've told our recruiting folks, if they come from your program, add a letter to that, go up.
So your Cs are my Bs, and that's fine.
That's high praise.
I like that, yeah.
Yeah, it was great.
Well, you know, there's a big satellite antenna next to Tom, so that was given to us.
And we used that until I left, I guess.
I hesitate to open the door and see what's inside, because I know it hasn't been used since.
But, yeah, I mean, it was great.
It was great.
How did you keep up with, since the technology was changing so quickly, how did you keep up with that?
Yeah, well, that was strenuous, I would say.
One thing is conferences.
I would go in the summer and sometimes during the year as well.
Big telecoms, some of them at the national level,
conferences and people present their new stuff and you meet people that can help you.
If you have any questions, just give me a call, do it.
A lot of that I didn't know.
You have to learn.
